instruction: Which sentence fits the situation?
prompt: You're in a meeting. The client asks why the dashboard isn't ready yet.
options: We've had some issues with the API, so it's delayed.
We had some issues with the API, so it's delayed.
We were having some issues with the API, so it's delayed.
explanation: The present perfect links a past event to NOW. The issues matter because they explain the current delay. The simple past would frame them as a closed episode, disconnected from the present.
compare: We had issues last week, but we fixed them. (closed)
We've had issues, so it's late. (still relevant now)
optionNotes: Possible, but it presents the issues as finished and disconnected from the delay.
The continuous focuses on the background activity, not its result now.

instruction: Fill the gap with one word.
prompt: I've been working on this project ___ three months, and it's finally taking shape.
explanation: “For” + a duration (three months). “Since” + a starting point (since March). French “depuis” covers both, which is why French speakers mix them up.
compare: I've lived here for three years.

trap.wrong: I have lived here since three years.
trap.correct: I have lived here for three years.
trap.explanation: “Since” introduces a starting point, “for” a duration. French “depuis” covers both.

instruction: Translate into natural English.
prompt: Ça fait deux ans que j'étudie l'informatique.
answers: I have been studying computer science for two years.
I've been studying computer science for two years.
I have studied computer science for two years.
I've studied computer science for two years.
model: I've been studying computer science for two years.
explanation: French uses the present (“j'étudie”) because the action continues. English marks that continuity with the present perfect (continuous), not the present simple.

trap.wrong: I study computer science since two years.
trap.correct: I've been studying computer science for two years.
trap.explanation: An action that started in the past and continues now takes the present perfect in English, not the present.

instruction: Correct the sentence.
prompt: I am agree with you on the main point, but not on the details.
answers: I agree with you on the main point, but not on the details.
model: I agree with you on the main point, but not on the details.
explanation: “Agree” is a verb, not an adjective. French “être d'accord” pushes you towards “be + agree”.

trap.explanation: “Agree” is already a verb: no “be” needed. French “être d'accord” causes the error.

instruction: Click the part that contains an error (or “No error”).
explanation: “Explain” doesn't take an indirect object directly: you explain something TO someone. Same pattern: describe, suggest, recommend.
compare: Could you explain it to me?
Could you explain how it works?

trap.wrong: Could you explain me how it works?
trap.correct: Could you explain to me how it works?
trap.explanation: You explain something TO someone. “Explain me” copies French “m'expliquer”.
trap.frenchHint: Tu peux m'expliquer comment ça marche ?

instruction: Choose the correct ending for a professional email.
prompt: I look forward to ___ from you.
explanation: Here “to” is a preposition (look forward TO something), not part of an infinitive. After a preposition, English uses the -ing form.

trap.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
trap.correct: I look forward to hearing from you.
trap.explanation: “To” in “look forward to” is a preposition, so it's followed by -ing.

instruction: Fill in the preposition.
prompt: Whether we go ahead depends entirely ___ the results of the pilot.
explanation: English says “depend on” (the idea of resting on something). French “dépendre de” makes “depend of” very tempting.

instruction: Which sentence is correct for this meaning?
prompt: Meaning: I didn't take the internship last year, and that's why I don't have experience now.
options: If I took the internship, I would have experience now.
If I had taken the internship, I would have experience now.
If I had taken the internship, I would have had experience now.
explanation: A mixed conditional: a PAST condition (had taken) with a PRESENT result (would have now). Each half keeps the time it refers to.
compare: If I had taken it, I would have learned a lot. (past → past)
If I were more organised, I would have finished. (present trait → past result)

instruction: Rewrite starting with “Hardly”.
prompt: The meeting had just started when the power went out.
answers: Hardly had the meeting started when the power went out.
Hardly had the meeting begun when the power went out.
model: Hardly had the meeting started when the power went out.
explanation: Negative or restrictive adverbs placed first (Hardly, Rarely, Never, Not only) trigger question-style word order: auxiliary before subject. It adds emphasis and a literary/formal tone. “Hardly… when”, but “No sooner… than”.
compare: No sooner had the meeting started than the power went out.

instruction: Rewrite starting with “Not only”.
prompt: The new policy reduces costs and it also improves employee satisfaction.
answers: Not only does the new policy reduce costs, but it also improves employee satisfaction.
Not only does the new policy reduce costs, it also improves employee satisfaction.
Not only does the new policy reduce costs but it also improves employee satisfaction.
mustAvoid: not only the new policy reduces
model: Not only does the new policy reduce costs, but it also improves employee satisfaction.
explanation: “Not only” at the start inverts the first clause (does + subject + base verb). The inversion signals emphasis: useful in argumentative writing.

instruction: Choose the most appropriate form for a formal report.
prompt: The committee recommends that each applicant ___ a portfolio.
explanation: After verbs like recommend, insist, suggest, demand (and “it is essential that”), formal English uses the base form: the mandative subjunctive. British English often accepts “should submit”; “submits” sounds informal in this context.
compare: It is essential that he be informed.

instruction: Click the part that contains an error (or “No error”).
explanation: “Suggest” cannot take “someone + to do”. Use “suggest (that) someone do” or “suggest doing”.
compare: She suggested that I rewrite it.

trap.wrong: He suggested me to rewrite it.
trap.correct: He suggested that I rewrite it.
trap.explanation: “Suggest” is followed by “that + subject + verb” or by -ing, never “someone to do”.
trap.frenchHint: Il m'a suggéré de le réécrire.

instruction: Pick the best deduction.
prompt: The server logs show no requests after 3 a.m. Someone ___ the service down for maintenance.
explanation: Modal + have + past participle talks about the past. “Must have” = logical certainty; “should have” = criticism or expectation; “can't have” = impossibility.
compare: He can't have seen it: he was offline.

instruction: Put the verb in the correct form.
prompt: I wish my flatmate ___ (stop) leaving dishes in the sink. It drives me mad.
hint: An annoying habit you'd like to change
explanation: “Wish + would” expresses irritation about someone else's behaviour you want to change. “Wish + past simple” is for present states (I wish I had more time).
compare: I wish I knew the answer. (state)

instruction: Which sentence is correct in a general statement?
options: The technology is changing the society in profound ways.
Technology is changing society in profound ways.
The technology is changing society in profound ways.
explanation: For general, abstract ideas English uses NO article (technology, society, education). French uses “la technologie, la société”. Add “the” only when it's specific: “the technology behind ChatGPT”.

trap.wrong: The technology is changing the society.
trap.explanation: General abstract nouns take no article in English.

instruction: Click the part that contains an error (or “No error”).
explanation: “Information” is uncountable in English (so is advice, feedback, equipment, research). So: “it was useful”, “a piece of information”.

trap.explanation: Information, advice, feedback, research are uncountable: no -s.

instruction: Which sentence means “it's no longer strange for me”?
options: I used to work at night.
I'm used to working at night.
I use to work at night.
explanation: “Used to + verb” = a past habit that's over. “Be/get used to + -ing” = be accustomed to. The “to” in the second one is a preposition, hence -ing.

instruction: Rewrite using a conditional inversion (no “if”).
prompt: If it were not for her support, the project would have been abandoned.
answers: Were it not for her support, the project would have been abandoned.
Had it not been for her support, the project would have been abandoned.
mustInclude: ^(were it not|had it not been) for
model: Had it not been for her support, the project would have been abandoned.
explanation: Formal English can drop “if” and invert: Were it not for…, Had I known…, Should you need… Since the result is past, “Had it not been for” is the most precise here.

instruction: Complete with the correct form of “update”.
prompt: Your CV really needs ___ before you apply.
explanation: “Need + -ing” has a passive meaning (British, common in speech): the CV needs to be updated.

instruction: Choose the correct form.
prompt: I'd rather you ___ anyone about this yet.
explanation: “Would rather + another subject” takes the past tense for a present/future meaning. Same logic as “It's time we left” or “I wish you were here”: the past signals distance from reality.
